content: The pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, commonly referred to as PCV13 or Prevnar 13, is recommended to protect infants, toddlers, and certain older children and adults with specific health conditions from pneumococcal disease. Pneumococcal disease is caused by infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria, which can spread from person to person through close contact. This disease can result in serious health complications, including pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and meningitis. Meningitis, an infection of the protective covering of the brain, is relatively rare (less than 1 case per 100,000 people annually), but it can lead to severe outcomes such as deafness, brain damage, or even death. Among children, pneumococcal meningitis is fatal in approximately 1 out of 10 cases. Children under the age of two are at a higher risk for severe disease compared to older children. Additionally, individuals with certain medical conditions, those over the age of 65, and cigarette smokers are also at increased risk. Before the introduction of the vaccine, pneumococcal infections caused significant health issues in children under five years old in the United States, including over 700 cases of meningitis, 13,000 bloodstream infections, approximately 5 million ear infections, and about 200 deaths annually. Despite vaccination efforts, about 4,000 adults still die each year from pneumococcal infections. Some strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae are resistant to antibiotics, making prevention through vaccination even more critical. The PCV13 vaccine provides protection against 13 types of pneumococcal bacteria, which are responsible for most severe infections in children and about half of the infections in adults. It is routinely administered to children at 2, 4, 6, and 12–15 months of age, as this age group is at the highest risk for serious pneumococcal diseases. The vaccine may also be recommended for certain older children or adults, depending on their health status. A second type of pneumococcal vaccine, called PPSV23, may be given to some children and adults, including everyone over the age of 65. There is a separate Vaccine Information Statement available for PPSV23. Individuals who have had a life-threatening allergic reaction to a previous dose of PCV13, an earlier pneumococcal vaccine called PCV7 (Prevnar), or any vaccine containing diphtheria toxoid (e.g., DTaP) should not receive PCV13. Additionally, anyone with a severe allergy to any component of the vaccine should avoid it. If the person scheduled for vaccination is ill, the doctor may decide to postpone the shot. It is important to inform your doctor about any severe allergies or health conditions before vaccination. As with any medication, including vaccines, there is a possibility of side effects. These are usually mild and resolve on their own, but serious reactions can occur. Reported side effects of PCV13 vary by dose and age. In children, about half experience drowsiness, temporary loss of appetite, or redness and tenderness at the injection site. About one-third develop swelling at the injection site, and up to 1 in 10 may have a mild fever (over 102.2°F or 39°C). Up to 8 in 10 children may become fussy or irritable. Adults receiving the vaccine have reported redness, pain, and swelling at the injection site, as well as mild fever, fatigue, headache, chills, or muscle pain. Life-threatening allergic reactions to vaccines are extremely rare. If a serious reaction occurs, such as signs of a severe allergic reaction (e.g., hives, swelling of the face and throat, difficulty breathing, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, or weakness), it typically begins within minutes to a few hours after vaccination. In such cases, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or going to the nearest hospital. Otherwise, contact your doctor. Serious reactions should be reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). Your doctor may file this report, or you can do so yourself through the VAERS website or by calling 1-800-822-7967. Note that VAERS is only for reporting reactions and does not provide medical advice. The National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP), established in 1986, provides a way for individuals who believe they have been injured by a vaccine to file a claim. For more information, you can call 1-800-338-2382 or visit the VICP website. For additional information about the PCV13 vaccine, consult your doctor, contact your local or state health department, or reach out to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) by calling 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visiting the CDC website.
